description: Create a restore point (bypass the 24h frequency limit) before any run; engine also writes a JSON state snapshot.
explanation: Creates a Windows restore point before the first change (lifting the 24-hour limit for this one call) so you can roll back with System Restore. The engine does this itself.
whoBenefits: Users with a specific need
tradeoff: Needs System Protection turned on for C:. Takes a few seconds and some disk space; if it fails the run is aborted.

description: Enable daily periodic registry backup (RegIdleBackup).
explanation: Turns the periodic registry backup (RegIdleBackup task) back on so a copy of the registry hives is saved on a schedule.
whoBenefits: Users who want to control background tasks
tradeoff: Uses a little disk space and a short background task. Nothing is lost.

description: Set diagnostic data policy to minimum. Honoured as 0 only on Enterprise/Education; Pro/Home treat it as Required (1).
breaks: Insider builds need telemetry
measuredEffect: Microsoft-disclosed (secondhand, Win10 1703): Basic about 109-159 KB/day, Enhanced about 239-348 KB/day. Not a packet capture.
explanation: Sets the diagnostic data level to the minimum. On Windows 11 Pro and Home, 0 is treated as Required (1), so you cannot reach a true off state. Real traffic at Required is already tiny.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users on any edition; real 'off' only on Enterprise, Education or Server
tradeoff: On Windows 11 Pro/Home, 0 is treated as Required (1), so the real effect differs from the label; only Enterprise/Education honour 0. Microsoft warns that fully off omits Windows Update failure information.
managedDeviceImpact: Can conflict with the Intune diagnostics-data policy and with Windows Update for Business / Autopatch reporting, which need at least Required data.

description: Atlas also sets AllowTelemetry/MaxTelemetryAllowed under CurrentVersion\Policies and Wow6432Node plus AllowDeviceNameInTelemetry.
explanation: Writes the same diagnostic level to extra registry locations. It mostly duplicates the main policy and adds little on its own.
whoBenefits: Users who want the policy applied redundantly
tradeoff: Little extra effect; more keys to keep track of.
managedDeviceImpact: Can conflict with the Intune diagnostics-data policy and WUfB / Autopatch reporting.

description: Stop OneSettings configuration downloads.
explanation: Stops OneSettings configuration downloads. Microsoft says settings-win.data.microsoft.com sends no diagnostic data and is used for remote configuration, so blocking it saves almost nothing.
whoBenefits: Privacy purists
tradeoff: Microsoft advises against blocking this endpoint. It may delay remote fixes and feature config.

description: Hide feedback notifications.
explanation: Hides feedback pop-ups. A nuisance fix, not a traffic or CPU saver.
whoBenefits: Anyone annoyed by prompts
tradeoff: None meaningful.

description: Disable event transcript / mini trace slot and delete DiagTrack ETL logs.
explanation: Turns off the local diagnostic event transcript and mini trace slot, and marks the diagnostic-data toast as already shown.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: The Diagnostic Data Viewer keeps less history, and there is less local diagnostic data for Microsoft support to look at.

description: Disable WMI autologgers Diagtrack-Listener, SQMLogger, SetupPlatformTel.
explanation: Stops three background trace sessions (Diagtrack-Listener, SQMLogger, SetupPlatformTel) from starting at boot.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Less local diagnostic tracing for troubleshooting; takes effect after a restart. Admin tools that read those traces have nothing to read.

description: Disable Customer Experience Improvement Program.
explanation: Turns off the Customer Experience Improvement Program, which sends anonymous usage data to Microsoft.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Microsoft gets less usage data from this PC. No visible loss. A policy from your organisation may already set it.

description: Disable Windows Error Reporting.
breaks: No crash reports; harder to troubleshoot with Microsoft tooling
measuredEffect: not measured; Windows Error Reporting only sends data after a crash, so idle impact is nil
explanation: Turns off Windows Error Reporting so crash data is not collected or sent. It is a privacy choice, not a speed gain.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Lose crash dumps and Microsoft fix suggestions.

description: Outbound firewall block for DiagTrack and WerSvc services.

implementation.run: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Tool Block DiagTrack' -Direction Outbound -Action Block -Service DiagTrack; New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Tool Block WerSvc' -Direction Outbound -Action Block -Service WerSvc

explanation: Adds outbound firewall blocks for the telemetry and error reporting services. The data volume is small and Microsoft notes some traffic still appears in captures.
whoBenefits: Users who want a belt-and-braces block
tradeoff: Blocks the DiagTrack and WerSvc services from the network. Can break Windows Update diagnostics, error reporting and Windows Update for Business reporting.
managedDeviceImpact: Can interfere with Intune/Defender diagnostics and Windows Update reporting. Note: this entry is a firewall command, which the engine skips.

description: Opt out of .NET CLI and PowerShell telemetry (machine env vars).
explanation: Sets two machine-wide environment variables so the .NET command-line tools and PowerShell do not send usage telemetry.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: No loss for everyday use. Only affects developer tools, and only for programs started after the change.

description: Turn off ads, suggestions and silent app installs for the user (also apply to Default user hive).

revert.note: restoreSnapshot per value; stock is 1 or absent

measuredEffect: not measured; fewer ads and suggestions rather than speed. Areas rated 1 and 2.
explanation: Stops Windows from showing suggested apps, tips and promotions in Start, Settings and the lock screen, and from silently installing promoted apps. Mainly a cleaner desktop with a bit less background network traffic.
whoBenefits: Anyone annoyed by ads and suggestions in Windows, especially new installs
tradeoff: You stop seeing tips and suggested apps. Some of the policies are not supported on Pro per the Policy CSP table, and the policy does not cover every per-user Spotlight toggle.

description: Block consumer experiences / suggested app installs by policy.
explanation: Blocks consumer experiences, meaning auto-installed promotional apps that appear after setup or updates. Keeps Start tidy and avoids downloads you did not ask for.
whoBenefits: Fresh installs, shared PCs and Enterprise/Education editions
tradeoff: Microsoft honours this policy on Enterprise/Education; Pro behaviour is uncertain. Must be set within 15 minutes of install or baked into an image to take effect. Little performance gain.

description: Disable advertising ID, tailored experiences, ink/typing harvesting.
explanation: Turns off the advertising ID, tailored experiences based on diagnostic data, and implicit ink and typing collection.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Ads in apps become less personalised (they are not removed). Handwriting and typing suggestions may personalise less. The per-user (HKCU) parts apply to the user running the engine only.

description: Disable activity feed, publishing and upload of user activities.
explanation: Turns off the activity feed and stops this PC from publishing or uploading your activity history.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Features that resume activity across your devices stop working. History already collected is not deleted.
notes: Winutil lists EnableActivityFeed=1 which conflicts with the intent; 0 is used here.

description: Disable Cross-Device Platform.
breaks: Nearby sharing / cross-device resume
explanation: Turns off the Connected Devices Platform used for Nearby Sharing, Phone Link and cross-device features. A small service, so mainly a privacy benefit.
whoBenefits: Users with no Bluetooth/Nearby Sharing/Phone Link use
tradeoff: Nearby Sharing, Phone Link and some device pairing features stop working.

description: Stop tracking app launches for Start suggestions.
breaks: Start 'most used' list empty
explanation: Stops Windows from recording which apps you launch to rank Start suggestions. A privacy setting with no measurable speed change.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Start shows fewer personalized recommendations.

description: Remove Bing web results/Cortana/location use from Windows Search by policy.
measuredEffect: not measured; reports say Start search waits on Microsoft servers before showing local results, with the biggest gain on older PCs
explanation: Stops the Start menu from sending your typing to Bing and waiting for web results. Local apps and files then show up faster and web clutter goes away. One of the few shell tweaks you can actually feel.
whoBenefits: Anyone who uses Start search for apps and files, especially on older PCs and slow connections
tradeoff: You lose web answers in Start such as weather, unit conversion and web suggestions. On some builds DisableSearchBoxSuggestions does not fully suppress web results.

description: Stop online font provider downloads.
explanation: Stops Windows from downloading fonts on demand from Microsoft online font providers.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Documents that rely on a cloud font show a substitute font until you install it yourself.

description: Stop disk health model downloads.
explanation: Stops Windows from downloading updated disk-health prediction models.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Disk-health warnings use the model already on the PC, which may become slightly out of date.

description: Disable Find My Device.
breaks: Cannot locate a lost device
explanation: Disable Find My Device.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Cannot locate a lost device

description: Disable settings sync and block user override.
explanation: Disable settings sync and block user override.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Deny location access system-wide and disable lfsvc / map updates.
breaks: Find My Device, weather, maps, automatic time zone
explanation: Denies location access and disables map updates. A privacy gain more than a performance one.
whoBenefits: Desktop users who never need location
tradeoff: Breaks Maps, weather and Find My Device. Disabling GeoLocation reportedly breaks Start search on new accounts.

description: Stop genuine ticket generation.
breaks: Store genuine validation tickets may not be issued
explanation: Stop genuine ticket generation.
whoBenefits: Users with a specific need
tradeoff: Store genuine validation tickets may not be issued

description: Force-deny app access to camera, microphone, location.
breaks: Video calls, voice input, maps in UWP apps stop working
explanation: Force-deny app access to camera, microphone, location.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users
tradeoff: Video calls, voice input, maps in UWP apps stop working

description: Disable Defender cloud reporting / sample submission and MRT reporting.
measuredEffect: not measured. Microsoft describes the cloud payload as small and sent only when local engines cannot decide.
explanation: Turns off Defender cloud reporting and sample submission. Traffic is small, so you save almost nothing, while protection against new threats gets weaker.
whoBenefits: Almost no one for performance reasons
tradeoff: Reduces protection against new malware. Treat 'turn MAPS off to save traffic' claims as unmeasured.

description: Hide Security and Maintenance toasts.
explanation: Hides Security and Maintenance pop-up notifications. This reduces noise but also hides warnings.
whoBenefits: People who find those pop-ups annoying
tradeoff: You may miss useful security alerts.

description: Disable the Office Telemetry Agent scheduled tasks (explicit names only).
explanation: Turns off the scheduled tasks that run the Office Telemetry Agent (the optional Telemetry Dashboard collector). Only these four task names are touched. The Office Automatic Updates, ClickToRun Service Monitor and subscription tasks in the same folder are NOT touched. Microsoft Learn documents OfficeTelemetryAgentLogOn; the FallBack and 2016 variants are the same agent on other Office builds and are skipped if absent.
whoBenefits: Home or small-office users who do not use the Office Telemetry Dashboard
tradeoff: If your organisation uses the Office Telemetry Dashboard, this PC stops reporting to it. Office itself and its updates are unaffected.
managedDeviceImpact: Only relevant where an admin runs the Telemetry Dashboard; otherwise none.

description: Disable telemetry scheduled tasks (Appraiser, ProgramDataUpdater, CEIP, Chkdsk Proxy, WER QueueReporting).
measuredEffect: Anecdotal CPU and disk spikes up to about 20 minutes from CompatTelRunner; no benchmark. Areas rated 1 and 3; reconciled to 2.
explanation: Disables telemetry scheduled tasks such as the Compatibility Appraiser. These are the best-known source of CompatTelRunner CPU and disk bursts, so this is the telemetry tweak most likely to be noticed on weaker PCs.
whoBenefits: HDD, low-end or older PCs with startup or idle spikes
tradeoff: Windows upgrade readiness checks and feature-update gating can behave differently because the Compatibility Appraiser is disabled; Windows may re-enable the tasks. Evidence is forum and vendor articles, not Microsoft data.
managedDeviceImpact: The Appraiser feeds feature-update readiness and compatibility gating that Windows Update for Business / Autopatch can rely on; check with your admin.

description: Stop and disable Connected User Experiences and Telemetry.
measuredEffect: PCGH (May 2025, 7800X3D, standard vs Nano 11 debloat): average gaming FPS unchanged. Microsoft-disclosed telemetry volume at Required level about 100-160 KB/day (old, Win10 1703). Background reviewers report steadier memory but no numbers. Areas rated this 0-2; reconciled to 1.
explanation: Stops the telemetry service (Connected User Experiences and Telemetry). Windows Update, activation and Defender keep working. It is mainly a privacy measure: traffic is small and a controlled test showed no FPS change.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users; people who see CompatTelRunner or telemetry spikes
tradeoff: Pauses compatibility telemetry and Feedback Hub. May interfere with Insider enrollment. Windows can re-enable it after updates. Deleting the service (some scripts do) can block ESU enrollment; disabling is safer.

description: Disable WerSvc, PcaSvc, diagnosticshub collector, wercplsupport.
breaks: No Program Compatibility Assistant prompts, no crash reports
ram_or_perf_effect: Fewer background services; hard to quantify
explanation: Disables error reporting and the program compatibility assistant. These are small services that mostly sleep, so the saving is tiny.
whoBenefits: Privacy-focused users
tradeoff: No crash reports or compatibility prompts for old programs, which makes troubleshooting harder.

description: ReviOS extra set: WdiServiceHost, WdiSystemHost, dam, wisvc, Wecsvc.
breaks: Built-in troubleshooters, Insider enrollment; some are protected and need registry Start=4
explanation: Disables diagnostic policy hosts, desktop activity moderator, Insider service and event collector. Mostly idle services.
whoBenefits: Tweakers on gaming-only PCs
tradeoff: Built-in troubleshooters stop working; Insider builds break; the activity moderator also manages power behavior.

description: Disable OneSyncSvc (and per-user instances) and TrkWks.
breaks: Mail/Calendar/People sync, NTFS link tracking
explanation: Disables mail/contacts sync and link tracking. Small services.
whoBenefits: Users with no Mail/Calendar app sync
tradeoff: Mail, People and Calendar apps stop syncing.

description: Disable UCPD driver and its scheduled task (reboot needed).
breaks: Removes Microsoft default-app hijack protection
explanation: Disable UCPD driver and its scheduled task (reboot needed).
whoBenefits: Tweakers who want fewer background services
tradeoff: Removes Microsoft default-app hijack protection

description: Disable NetBT, GpuEnergyDrv, tcpipreg and Telemetry driver entries (registry Start=4, reboot).
breaks: NetBIOS name resolution, legacy SMB discovery; tcpipreg flagged experimental by ReviOS
explanation: Disable NetBT, GpuEnergyDrv, tcpipreg and Telemetry driver entries (registry Start=4, reboot).
whoBenefits: Tweakers who want fewer background services
tradeoff: NetBIOS name resolution, legacy SMB discovery; tcpipreg flagged experimental by ReviOS

description: Set the Edge updater service (edgeupdate) to Manual instead of disabling it.
explanation: Sets the Edge update service to start on demand instead of at boot. Edge still updates itself through its own scheduled update tasks; this does not disable updating.
whoBenefits: Everyone, as a safe default
tradeoff: Edge updates can be delayed if the updater tasks are also disabled; Manual alone normally does not stop updates.
managedDeviceImpact: Edge updates may be governed by Intune or Edge update policy; check with your admin.

description: Set the console driver (condrv) to start automatically (fix for error 0xd000003a).
measuredEffect: not measured; a stability fix, not a speed-up
explanation: Sets the Windows console driver service to start automatically. Reported as a fix for console apps failing with 0xd000003a after other services were changed. It is only useful if you hit that error.
whoBenefits: Only people who see error 0xd000003a in console apps
tradeoff: Changes a kernel-driver start type for a problem most PCs do not have.

description: Set WSAIFabricSvc to Manual (or Disabled) to avoid AI fabric autostart.
explanation: Stops the Windows AI Fabric service from starting automatically. Safe because Manual still allows on-demand start.
whoBenefits: PCs not using Windows AI features or without an NPU
tradeoff: None for most users. Disabled (rather than Manual) can break AI features. Only source is Win11Debloat release notes.

description: Winutil: CscService and SharedAccess Disabled.
breaks: Offline Files; Internet Connection Sharing, Hyper-V/WSL NAT
measuredEffect: not measured; catalog note: Reviewer measured 100 MB or less
explanation: Winutil: CscService and SharedAccess Disabled.
whoBenefits: Tweakers who want fewer background services
tradeoff: Offline Files; Internet Connection Sharing, Hyper-V/WSL NAT

description: Disable Microsoft Account Sign-in Assistant.
breaks: MSA sign-in, Store, Xbox, OneDrive auth
explanation: Disable Microsoft Account Sign-in Assistant.
whoBenefits: Tweakers who want fewer background services
tradeoff: MSA sign-in, Store, Xbox, OneDrive auth

description: Disable License Manager.
breaks: Store app licensing and installs
explanation: Disable License Manager.
whoBenefits: Tweakers who want fewer background services
tradeoff: Store app licensing and installs

description: Disable time sync (Type NoSync).
breaks: Clock drift breaks TLS, Kerberos, certificates
explanation: Disable time sync (Type NoSync).
whoBenefits: Tweakers who want fewer background services
tradeoff: Clock drift breaks TLS, Kerberos, certificates

description: Disable hibernation (and Fast Startup). Skip on laptops by default.
breaks: No hibernate; sleep heat on some modern-standby laptops (playbook #116, #199)
measuredEffect: not measured; frees the hibernation file disk space
explanation: Turns off hibernation, which also removes the hibernation file and disables Fast Startup. You get disk space back but lose hibernate and faster boots.
whoBenefits: Small-SSD desktops that never hibernate and need the disk space
tradeoff: Boots slower (same cost as disabling Fast Startup) and you lose hibernate. Bad for laptops.

description: Disable Fast Startup (hybrid boot).
ram_or_perf_effect: Clean cold boots; slightly slower boot on HDD
measuredEffect: Single-machine test: about 4 s boot with Fast Startup on vs about 9-10 s off (NVMe). Unverified estimate: 10-30 s slower depending on drive. Areas rated 0 and 1.; MakeUseOf (single author, SSD): shutdown-to-desktop about 11 s to 13 s
explanation: Makes Shut down a real full shutdown instead of a hybrid hibernate. This clears stale state and avoids odd issues with updates, drivers or dual boot. It is a stability / clean-boot tweak and makes boot SLOWER, not faster.
whoBenefits: People with dual boot, shutdown or update glitches
tradeoff: Slower boot from Shut down (about 4 s with Fast Startup on vs 9-10 s off in one NVMe test, more on slower disks). Restart is unaffected.

description: Create custom high-performance plan from the Ultimate Performance base and activate it (desktops only).
breaks: Higher idle power and heat; unsuitable for battery laptops
measuredEffect: ComputerBase 2017 (Ryzen 1800X, Win10, confounded with HPET): about 2% geometric mean, up to about 17% in one game, 0% in four titles; idle power 53 W vs 62 W. Mostly a core-parking issue on first-gen Ryzen, since fixed. No controlled modern frame-time data found.
explanation: Keeps the CPU at high clocks and stops it parking cores or dropping speed when idle, so there is less ramp-up delay when work arrives. On modern CPUs the average difference is usually within noise but it can reduce stutter in some CPU-bound scenes.
whoBenefits: Desktop users with latency-sensitive workloads (games, audio) who can accept higher idle power and heat
tradeoff: Higher idle power, heat and fan noise. Not for laptops on battery. Benchmark three runs per plan before keeping it.

description: Activate Balanced plan.
measuredEffect: Not measured on modern hardware; Balanced vs High Performance showed about 2% on a 2017 Ryzen setup, mostly from the old core-parking issue.
explanation: Restores the default Balanced plan, which saves power at idle. On current CPUs it gives almost the same gaming speed as high-performance plans.
whoBenefits: Laptops and anyone who wants lower idle power and noise without losing real gaming speed
tradeoff: Possibly a few percent lower in rare CPU-bound scenes on some systems.

description: Disable memory compression (reboot).
breaks: More paging on low-RAM systems
ram_or_perf_effect: Slight CPU saving, slightly more RAM use
measuredEffect: not measured as a gain; Microsoft Q&A report of about 1 GB held by compression on 16 GB, and disabling it increases pagefile use
explanation: Disables RAM compression. It trades a little CPU for memory pressure, with no benchmark showing a gaming gain. It can hurt on 8 GB machines.
whoBenefits: Systems with 32 GB or more where it is harmless but unneeded
tradeoff: More paging on low-RAM systems. Disabling compression worsens commit and paging pressure, because pages that were compressed in RAM go to the pagefile instead.

description: Disable NTFS last-access updates.
measuredEffect: not measured; catalog note: Fewer metadata writes
explanation: Stops NTFS from updating the last-accessed time stamp each time a file is read, which saves a few small disk writes.
whoBenefits: Users who want to fine-tune Windows behaviour
tradeoff: Last-access times are no longer reliable; some backup, search and forensic tools that use them behave differently. Takes effect after a restart.

description: Disable 8.3 short-name creation.
breaks: Legacy installers / backup tools relying on 8.3 names
explanation: Disable 8.3 short-name creation.
whoBenefits: Users who want to fine-tune Windows behaviour
tradeoff: Legacy installers / backup tools relying on 8.3 names

description: Raise SvcHostSplitThresholdInKB so services share svchost processes (reboot).
breaks: One shared-host crash takes more services down; XboxGipSvc breaks under naive grouping
measuredEffect: fewer processes in Task Manager; in controlled debloat tests RAM saved was within 100-200 MB at most
explanation: Lets services share svchost processes so the Task Manager list looks shorter. Total memory used barely changes, and a crash in one service can take more with it.
whoBenefits: Mostly cosmetic
tradeoff: Less isolation between services, harder troubleshooting. Placebo for performance.

description: Foreground priority boost (38 / 0x26).
measuredEffect: not measured; no controlled FPS, frametime or input-lag benchmark of 0x26 (38) vs the default found on Win10 or Win11
explanation: Windows already gives the window you are using a short priority boost. This setting changes how long programs run before the scheduler switches. 0x26 is what the Control Panel 'best performance for programs' option writes, so it is safe, but nobody has shown a measurable gain.
whoBenefits: Users who run one heavy foreground app on a saturated CPU; most people will not notice
tradeoff: Background tasks such as indexing or encoding get a little less CPU while you work. Community advice on 'best' values is trial and error, not data.

description: Shorten shutdown/hang timeouts, zero menu delay.
breaks: Apps killed before saving on shutdown (AutoEndTasks)
measuredEffect: not measured; only a perceived speedup is reported for MenuShowDelay=0 (default commonly cited as 400 ms)
explanation: Shortens how long Windows waits for stuck apps and services at shutdown, and removes the hover delay before cascading menus open. The menu part is cosmetic and only affects classic Win32 menus.
whoBenefits: Users whose shutdowns hang on unresponsive apps, or who dislike the cascading menu delay
tradeoff: Shorter shutdown timeouts can cut off apps that are still saving data. Submenus may open accidentally while moving the mouse.

description: Disable Game DVR background recording.
measuredEffect: Laptopmedia (GTA V, MX150 laptop): about 0.3 FPS difference while recording, within run noise.
explanation: Turns off Game DVR background recording and the Game Bar capture hooks. The measured FPS cost of recording is tiny, so the gain is small, mostly on weak PCs.
whoBenefits: Low-end or budget systems, and anyone who never uses Xbox Game Bar clips
tradeoff: You lose Win+Alt+R clip capture and Game Bar recording. Fast, safe and easily reversed.

description: Block UWP background apps.
breaks: Alarms/mail/live tiles stop in background
measuredEffect: Debloat-tool tests saved at most 100-200 MB RAM in total. Windows 10 Game Mode tests: about +6 fps only under heavy background load, 0-1 fps on clean systems. One guide reports 187 to 141 background processes combined with many other changes.
explanation: Stops Store apps from running in the background when you are not using them. Helps most on PCs with many Store apps installed.
whoBenefits: Laptops and low-RAM PCs with many Store apps
tradeoff: Live tiles, notifications and mail/calendar sync from Store apps may be delayed.

description: Stop Explorer folder-type auto detection.
breaks: Clearing Bags/BagMRU loses per-folder view customisations (back up first)
explanation: Stops Explorer from scanning folder contents to pick a view. In folders with very many files this can cut the delay when a folder first opens.
whoBenefits: Anyone with huge folders that open slowly in Explorer
tradeoff: Folders may not pick the best view automatically, so you set views by hand.

description: Disable Fault Tolerant Heap.
breaks: No automatic heap shims for crashing apps
explanation: Disables a feature that applies fixes to apps that keep crashing. It does not raise FPS and removes a stability helper.
whoBenefits: Almost no one
tradeoff: Crashing apps no longer get automatic mitigation.

description: Disable Sleep Study diagnostic logs.
explanation: Disable Sleep Study diagnostic logs.
whoBenefits: Users who want to fine-tune Windows behaviour
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Disable Reserved Storage (~7 GB).
breaks: Feature updates may fail on low disk space
measuredEffect: not measured; catalog note: Frees about 7 GB disk
explanation: Disable Reserved Storage (~7 GB).
whoBenefits: Users who want to fine-tune Windows behaviour
tradeoff: Feature updates may fail on low disk space

description: Disable Storage Sense auto-cleanup.
breaks: Temp/Recycle Bin not auto-purged
explanation: Turns off Storage Sense, which automatically deletes temp files and old Recycle Bin items. By default Storage Sense only runs when disk space is low, so turning it off has no performance benefit and removes the low-disk cleanup.
whoBenefits: Users who want to fine-tune Windows behaviour
tradeoff: Temp files and the Recycle Bin are no longer cleaned automatically, so disk space is freed less often.

description: Delete user and system temp files (best effort).
breaks: Running installers or updates can fail if their working files are deleted.
explanation: Deletes everything in your temp folder and in C:\Windows\Temp. It frees disk space, but files cannot be restored.
whoBenefits: People who want to reclaim a little disk space
tradeoff: Not reversible. Can remove in-flight installer or Intune Management Extension working files, and files an open program still needs.
managedDeviceImpact: Can disturb app installs or Intune Management Extension runs that are in progress.

description: Component store cleanup with /ResetBase.
breaks: Cannot uninstall superseded updates
explanation: Component store cleanup with /ResetBase.
whoBenefits: Users who want to fine-tune Windows behaviour
tradeoff: Cannot uninstall superseded updates

description: Legacy F8 boot menu policy.
explanation: Legacy F8 boot menu policy.
whoBenefits: Users who want to fine-tune Windows behaviour
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Disable peer-to-peer Delivery Optimization (0 HTTP only; 99 simple also acceptable).
measuredEffect: 2Pint 25-client enterprise LAN test: default DO moved 26 GB, basic tuning 14 GB, tuned plus DNS-SD 11 GB over 4 hours (download side, forced updates). Measures an enterprise LAN, not a home PC; no consumer upload measurement exists.
explanation: Stops your PC from sharing update files with other PCs on the internet. This is one of the few tweaks with a documented effect on bandwidth, mainly your upload.
whoBenefits: Home users on slow or capped upstream links; metered connections
tradeoff: Microsoft says turning DO off does not stop downloads. On a LAN, peering can reduce WAN traffic, so mode 0 can raise it. Mode 100 is deprecated and can cause error 0x80d03002.

description: Sync W32Time from pool.ntp.org (skip on domain-joined).
breaks: Do not apply on domain-joined machines
explanation: Points the Windows clock at pool.ntp.org instead of the default Microsoft time server.
whoBenefits: Users with specific network needs
tradeoff: Do not use on domain-joined machines. The engine always skips this on managed devices because time sync is controlled by organisation policy.

description: Disable IPv6 components.
breaks: Some VPNs, Xbox networking; Microsoft advises against
explanation: Disable IPv6 components.
whoBenefits: Users with specific network needs
tradeoff: Some VPNs, Xbox networking; Microsoft advises against

description: Disable Teredo.
breaks: Some Xbox features, DO peering
explanation: Disable Teredo.
whoBenefits: Users with specific network needs
tradeoff: Some Xbox features, DO peering

description: Disable NCSI active probe.
breaks: Captive portal detection misreports
measuredEffect: Single small HTTP GET per network change event
explanation: Stops the small web check Windows uses to decide whether you are online. That probe is a tiny request, so the saving is negligible.
whoBenefits: Isolated networks or privacy purists
tradeoff: Windows may show 'no internet' and some apps misbehave.

description: Stop automatic maps data download.
explanation: Stops automatic download of offline maps. Documented by Microsoft and harmless, but it only matters if you have downloaded maps.
whoBenefits: Metered or slow connections with offline maps installed
tradeoff: Offline maps in the Maps app stay out of date. Do not disable the MapsBroker service instead.

description: Prevent device metadata retrieval from network.
explanation: Stops Windows from downloading device icons and descriptions from the internet when you plug in hardware.
whoBenefits: Users with specific network needs
tradeoff: New hardware may show a generic name or icon in Devices and Printers. Drivers still install normally.

description: Restrict anonymous SAM/share enumeration.
explanation: Stops anonymous (not signed-in) network users from listing account names and shares on this PC. A standard hardening setting.
whoBenefits: Users with specific network needs
tradeoff: Old tools and some legacy devices that browse shares anonymously stop being able to list them. Signed-in access is unaffected.
managedDeviceImpact: Often already set by a security baseline or Group Policy; the two values here may be overwritten at the next policy refresh.

description: Disable SMB client bandwidth throttling (command step; skipped by the engine).
explanation: Turns off the SMB client bandwidth throttle. This catalog entry is reference only: the engine never runs free-form commands, so it is skipped.
whoBenefits: People who copy large files over SMB on fast LANs
tradeoff: Higher peak load on the network from SMB transfers.

description: Disable Recall / AI data analysis snapshots by policy (+ optional feature).
ram_or_perf_effect: Avoids snapshot disk/CPU use on Copilot+ PCs
measuredEffect: not measured; no CPU/RAM/disk numbers found. Qualitative reports only (early Insider build felt slow).
explanation: Turns off Recall, which takes periodic screenshots of your screen. The policy stops snapshots being saved and deletes ones already saved. The main win is privacy, not speed.
whoBenefits: Anyone on a Copilot+ PC or 24H2 Pro/Enterprise who does not want a searchable screen history on disk
tradeoff: You lose the Recall timeline. Policy needs 24H2 with KB5055627 or later. Microsoft's page is inconsistent about Recall's default on managed devices, so check the result.

description: Disable Windows Copilot by policy and hide the taskbar button (registry only, fully reversible).
measuredEffect: not measured; Microsoft says TurnOffWindowsCopilot does not control the newer Copilot app (24H2 and later)
explanation: Sets the old Windows Copilot policy and hides the Copilot taskbar button. Microsoft marks TurnOffWindowsCopilot as deprecated and says it does not cover the newer Copilot app, so on 24H2 and later only the taskbar button change is reliably visible. App removal is a separate, irreversible tweak (ai-copilot-app-remove).
whoBenefits: Anyone who does not use Copilot and wants a cleaner taskbar
tradeoff: The policy may do nothing on current builds; the taskbar button is hidden but the Copilot app stays installed. Microsoft: the TurnOffWindowsCopilot policy is subject to near-term deprecation; AppLocker is the documented replacement.

description: Remove the Copilot app packages (no exact undo).

steps.how: winget/Store, or Add-AppxPackage -Register saved InstallLocation manifest

measuredEffect: press measurement (Windows Latest, 2026-04): new Copilot app about 500 MB in background, about 1 GB active; previous native app under 100 MB
explanation: Removes the Copilot app packages for all users and from the provisioning list. The engine skips AppX steps unless -AllowIrreversible is passed.
whoBenefits: Anyone who never uses Copilot
tradeoff: No exact undo: reinstall from the Microsoft Store. Updates or the Store can bring the app back.

description: Disable Click to Do.
explanation: Disables Click to Do, the overlay that lets you act on text or images on screen. It only runs on demand, so this mainly removes an entry point and AI features you did not ask for.
whoBenefits: People who want fewer AI hooks in the shell
tradeoff: Insider-only per Microsoft Learn; no effect on release builds until it ships. Support depends on your build.

description: Uninstall OneDrive (only when no account configured; undo Known Folder Move first).
breaks: Desktop/Documents redirection left pointing at OneDrive; data loss risk
measuredEffect: not measured; one process, roughly tens of MB when idle
explanation: Removes OneDrive if you do not use it. Saves a small background process and stops the sign-in nags.
whoBenefits: People with no OneDrive account
tradeoff: If Desktop/Documents are backed up to OneDrive, uninstalling can strand files. Some guides advise leaving it alone.

description: Disable OneDrive file sync by policy.
breaks: Sync and Known Folder Backup stop
explanation: Blocks OneDrive file sync by policy. Stops sync traffic but OneDrive stays installed.
whoBenefits: Managed or offline-only PCs
tradeoff: Cloud backup and Files On-Demand stop working.

description: Block consumer Teams auto-install.
measuredEffect: Teams plus Widgets about 0.5-1.0 GB on one low-end laptop (single machine). Microsoft documents the setting for setup time only.
explanation: Stops the consumer Teams app from installing itself and starting at login. Teams can launch WebView2 processes at sign-in. Saves nothing if it is already installed.
whoBenefits: Home users who do not use Teams, and low-RAM PCs
tradeoff: Consumer Teams must be installed manually later. Little effect on an already-installed image; Microsoft documents no runtime policy for this on Pro.

description: Remove IE, Steps Recorder, legacy Media Player, WordPad, Math Recognizer (resolve exact names first).
explanation: Remove IE, Steps Recorder, legacy Media Player, WordPad, Math Recognizer (resolve exact names first).
whoBenefits: Users who do not use the component
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Force-remove Edge via external tool (EdgeRemover/--force-uninstall); fragile, unsupported outside EEA.
breaks: WebView2 apps, Widgets, Search, Office features; Windows Update may reinstall
explanation: Force-removes Edge. The Edge background processes are better handled by policies, and removal is fragile.
whoBenefits: Almost nobody
tradeoff: Unsupported, can break WebView2 apps, Widgets and Help. Win11Debloat authors also advise against it.

description: Disable Store apps / auto-download.
breaks: App installs and updates
explanation: Disables the Store and its auto-downloads. Microsoft states this also stops app updates and the Store itself, a big functional cost for little traffic saved.
whoBenefits: Locked-down kiosks
tradeoff: Breaks the Store and app updates.

description: Edge policy debloat: sidebar, shopping assistant, startup boost, background mode, metrics, personalization reporting.
measuredEffect: Policies are documented by Microsoft but no memory figure is given; a third-party guide estimates hundreds of MB for Startup Boost while Edge is closed (unmeasured).
explanation: Uses documented Edge policies to hide the sidebar and Copilot button, stop the shopping assistant, stop Edge pre-loading at sign-in (Startup Boost) and stop it staying alive after you close it (background mode).
whoBenefits: Anyone with Edge installed, especially on 8 GB machines
tradeoff: Edge opens a little slower from cold. Background sessions and push notifications from web apps stop when Edge is closed. Sidebar tools are lost.

description: Edge privacy policies: no search suggestions/autofill, DNT, hide first run.
explanation: Edge privacy policies: no search suggestions/autofill, DNT, hide first run.
whoBenefits: Edge users with specific preferences
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Disable Edge password manager.
explanation: Disable Edge password manager.
whoBenefits: Edge users with specific preferences
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Disable Edge SmartScreen.
explanation: Disable Edge SmartScreen.
whoBenefits: Edge users with specific preferences
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Remove consumer/promo AppX + provisioned copies (allowlist; never Store, App Installer, Security, shell, runtimes).

revert.how: winget/Store, or Add-AppxPackage -Register saved InstallLocation manifest

breaks: Some apps return after updates; Atlas Deprovisioned keys may block reinstall (delete per-package key)
ram_or_perf_effect: Mostly disk; Yahoo test found idle RAM barely changes
explanation: Removes promotional and consumer apps from the machine and the provisioning list so they do not come back for new users. Mostly frees disk space and clutter, not speed.
whoBenefits: Fresh installs and shared machines
tradeoff: New Outlook is documented as impossible to block from installing on builds after 23H2, so it may return; use provisioned-package removal.

description: Remove Widgets platform packages (policy Dsh AllowNewsAndInterests=0 is the reversible alternative).

steps.how: winget/Store, or Add-AppxPackage -Register saved InstallLocation manifest

breaks: StartExperiencesApp removal can alter Start; Widgets removal touches shared packages
measuredEffect: Widgets plus Teams about 0.5-1.0 GB on one low-end laptop; a controlled debloat test saved at most 100-200 MB overall. No controlled test for Widgets alone.
explanation: Deletes the Widgets packages. The same result is available with an official policy that can be undone, and updates may bring the packages back.
whoBenefits: Users who never open Widgets
tradeoff: Harder to undo than the policy, and may be reinstalled by updates. Do not remove the WebView2 runtime. Prefer the policy tweak.

description: Remove Xbox / gaming packages.

revert.how: winget/Store, or Add-AppxPackage -Register saved InstallLocation manifest

breaks: Game Bar, Xbox sign-in in games, Game Pass; ReviOS keeps Xbox by default
measuredEffect: PCGH (May 2025) standard vs Nano 11 debloat showed no gaming change; no benchmark shows a gain from removing Xbox apps. Background area rated 1, gaming area 0.
explanation: Removes Xbox apps and services. The savings are small and no benchmark shows a gain; removal can break Game Pass, Store games and Xbox sign-in.
whoBenefits: PCs that never play Store or Game Pass games and want a cleaner app list
tradeoff: Xbox Identity and Gaming Services are needed by many games. The Win11Debloat wiki recommends a repair tool if you need them back.

description: Opt-in removal of utility apps: Paint, Terminal, Camera, Sticky Notes, Alarms, Sound Recorder, Quick Assist, Snipping Tool, Calculator.

revert.how: winget/Store, or Add-AppxPackage -Register saved InstallLocation manifest

breaks: Removes useful tools; never remove Terminal if running from it
explanation: Removing Paint and similar utilities frees a little disk space only. If your reason is Paint's AI, the Paint policies are a safer way to switch the AI off while keeping the app.
whoBenefits: Nobody gains speed from this; only people who want the tools gone
tradeoff: You lose handy tools. Prefer the Paint AI policies instead.

description: Remove OEM packages (HP, Lenovo, Dell).
breaks: OEM driver/firmware utilities
explanation: Remove OEM packages (HP, Lenovo, Dell).
whoBenefits: Users who want a cleaner app list
tradeoff: OEM driver/firmware utilities

description: Remove Phone Link / CrossDevice (use separate step; do not bulk remove).

revert.how: winget/Store, or Add-AppxPackage -Register saved InstallLocation manifest

explanation: Removes Phone Link. The app only runs when used or paired, so little is saved. Microsoft documents no policy for this, so removal is the only route.
whoBenefits: Users who do not pair a phone
tradeoff: Lose Phone Link, notification mirroring and file transfer to the phone. Reinstallable from the Store.

description: Restore Windows 10 right-click menu (restart Explorer).
explanation: Brings back the full Windows 10 right-click menu so you do not have to click Show more options. Saves a click; some people find it opens faster, but there is no measurement.
whoBenefits: Power users who use right-click actions often
tradeoff: Overrides the new compact menu, and a future update may change it. Needs an Explorer restart.

description: Dark mode, transparency off (cosmetic).
measuredEffect: DWM composition adds roughly one frame of latency (author's own estimate); the original 8 ms vs 17 ms figures were largely retracted in a 2020 update
explanation: Switches Windows and apps to the dark theme and turns off transparency effects. Cosmetic: the claimed latency benefit was largely retracted by its author, so no speed gain is claimed.
whoBenefits: Low-end or integrated GPU systems, or people who prefer the look
tradeoff: Loses the translucent look of Start, the taskbar and Settings; changes the look of every app that follows the system theme.

description: Add End Task to taskbar menu.
explanation: Adds an End task option to the taskbar right-click menu so you can close a frozen app quickly. Does not speed anything up but makes recovery from hangs faster.
whoBenefits: Anyone who often deals with frozen apps
tradeoff: A quick way to kill an app can discard unsaved work.

description: Disable 5x-Shift Sticky Keys popup.
explanation: Stops the Sticky Keys prompt when you tap Shift five times. A pure annoyance fix, useful for gamers.
whoBenefits: Gamers and fast typists
tradeoff: Loses the shortcut for people who rely on Sticky Keys for accessibility.

description: Show file extensions.
explanation: Shows file extensions like .exe and .pdf. A safety and clarity tweak, not a speed one; helps spot disguised files.
whoBenefits: Everyone, especially for spotting fake file types
tradeoff: None meaningful.

description: Disable Windows Chat icon and Widgets (policy).
measuredEffect: One author's laptop: roughly 0.5-1.0 GB extra memory with default Teams and Widgets. Controlled debloat test: at most 100-200 MB saved overall. Conflict noted; Microsoft gives no figure.
explanation: Turns off Widgets and the Chat icon with Microsoft's supported policy. Widgets stops running its background processes and news feed. A clean, reversible, supported way to do it.
whoBenefits: Low-RAM PCs (under 8 GB) and anyone who does not use Widgets
tradeoff: No weather or news panel. The Chat icon policy is Enterprise/Education only. The Windows Feeds EnableFeeds value is Windows 10 only; the Dsh AllowNewsAndInterests part does the work.

description: Remove 'Edit with Paint 3D' context entries.

implementation.run: foreach($e in '.3mf','.bmp','.fbx','.gif','.jfif','.jpe','.jpeg','.jpg','.png','.tif','.tiff'){reg export then reg delete HKCR\SystemFileAssociations\$e\Shell\3D Edit}

explanation: Removes the Edit with Paint 3D entry from the right-click menu of image files.
whoBenefits: Users who want a tidier interface
tradeoff: The menu entry disappears (the Paint 3D app stays installed) and an update may bring it back. The engine currently skips this entry because it is a command step.

description: Defer feature updates 30-365 days; quality/security updates keep flowing.
breaks: Update-ring settings from Intune or Group Policy can be overridden or can override this.
explanation: Delays feature updates (the yearly Windows version upgrades) by 30 days using the Windows Update policy keys. Monthly security and quality updates are not delayed.
whoBenefits: Users who need control over update timing
tradeoff: Conflicts with Intune/WUfB update rings or Autopatch; feature updates arrive 30 days late.
managedDeviceImpact: Conflicts with Intune update rings / Windows Autopatch; the engine already skips the updates category on managed devices.

description: No forced reboot while a user is signed in.
breaks: Patches stay pending until manual reboot
explanation: No forced reboot while a user is signed in.
whoBenefits: Users who need control over update timing
tradeoff: Patches stay pending until manual reboot

description: Block drivers from WU quality updates.
breaks: Missed vendor drivers
explanation: Block drivers from WU quality updates.
whoBenefits: Users who need control over update timing
tradeoff: Missed vendor drivers

description: Disable Store auto-download and app archiving.
breaks: Store apps stop auto-updating
explanation: Stops the Store updating apps in the background. Saves some network and disk activity.
whoBenefits: Metered connections
tradeoff: Apps get outdated and miss security fixes unless you update manually.

description: NoAutoUpdate policy / pause updates (opt-in only).
breaks: No security patches until reverted; recovery issues reported after Atlas
explanation: NoAutoUpdate policy / pause updates (opt-in only).
whoBenefits: Users who need control over update timing
tradeoff: No security patches until reverted; recovery issues reported after Atlas

description: Disable wuauserv/UsoSvc (never WaaSMedicSvc).
breaks: No updates; leaving WaaSMedicSvc disabled breaks Store/AppX
explanation: Disable wuauserv/UsoSvc (never WaaSMedicSvc).
whoBenefits: Users who need control over update timing
tradeoff: No updates; leaving WaaSMedicSvc disabled breaks Store/AppX

description: DisableAntiSpyware policy, wscsvc Start=4 (Tamper Protection must be off first; do not bypass).
breaks: No real-time protection; Defender re-enables on updates
explanation: DisableAntiSpyware policy, wscsvc Start=4 (Tamper Protection must be off first; do not bypass).
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: No real-time protection; Defender re-enables on updates

description: Disable SmartScreen (system, Explorer, AppHost, Edge legacy).
explanation: Disable SmartScreen (system, Explorer, AppHost, Edge legacy).
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Turn Smart App Control off. IRREVERSIBLE without reset.
explanation: Turn Smart App Control off. IRREVERSIBLE without reset.
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Disable VBS / Memory Integrity / Credential Guard (reboot). Windows may re-enable from Oct 2026.
breaks: Loses kernel code-integrity and driver defences
ram_or_perf_effect: 0% on Cinebench, roughly 7-15% on some older gaming PCs (secondhand)
measuredEffect: ComputerBase (Nov 2023, Win11 22H2): HVCI on/off can mean double-digit differences in CPU-limited scenes. Tom's Hardware (secondhand): about 5-7% average, up to 15% 1% lows with VBS on in 12th-gen tests; worst cases about 30% on older CPUs without MBEC.
explanation: Memory Integrity (HVCI) runs a security layer under Windows using virtualization. It can cost frame rate in CPU-limited games, mostly on older processors. It has a real measured effect, but switches off a significant protection.
whoBenefits: Owners of older CPUs or high-refresh CPU-bound esports setups who measured a gain on their own games
tradeoff: Removes kernel code-integrity and driver protections. Windows may turn it back on. Test your own games and keep it on for a general-use PC.

description: Disable CPU/OS exploit mitigations.
explanation: Turns off CPU exploit mitigations such as those for Spectre-class flaws. No gaming benchmark was found, and modern CPUs have hardware fixes, so the gain is small.
whoBenefits: Almost no one; only very old CPUs might see a gain
tradeoff: Exposes the system to known CPU side-channel attacks. Not recommended.

description: No secure-desktop dimming for UAC prompts.
explanation: No secure-desktop dimming for UAC prompts.
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Prevent automatic device encryption (never decrypt existing drives).
breaks: No silent encryption or key escrow
explanation: Prevent automatic device encryption (never decrypt existing drives).
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: No silent encryption or key escrow

description: Decrypt system drive.
explanation: Decrypt system drive.
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Disable automatic root certificate update.
explanation: Stops automatic root certificate updates. Microsoft says this should not be disabled and the savings are tiny.
whoBenefits: Nobody in normal use
tradeoff: Reduces security and can cause certificate errors.

description: Disable Windows Platform Binary Table execution.
breaks: OEM firmware-injected tools stop auto-running
explanation: Disable Windows Platform Binary Table execution.
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: OEM firmware-injected tools stop auto-running

description: Disable Remote Assistance.
explanation: Turns off Windows Remote Assistance invitations (msra).
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: Nobody can offer or request help through Remote Assistance. Quick Assist and Remote Desktop are separate and unaffected; helpdesk tools that rely on Remote Assistance stop working.

description: Block Microsoft account sign-in.
breaks: Store, Xbox, OneDrive, anything needing MSA
explanation: Block Microsoft account sign-in.
whoBenefits: Only users with a specific need; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: Store, Xbox, OneDrive, anything needing MSA

description: EnableLinkedConnections for mapped drives under elevation.
breaks: Weaker UAC isolation.
explanation: Makes mapped network drives visible to both elevated and non-elevated processes by linking the two access tokens. That weakens the isolation UAC provides.
whoBenefits: Admins who need mapped drives to show up in elevated prompts
tradeoff: Weakens UAC token isolation: a non-elevated program can see what an elevated one maps.

description: Execution policy RemoteSigned (LocalMachine). Relaxes the Windows client default.
breaks: Weaker defence against malicious local scripts.
explanation: Changes the PowerShell execution policy for the whole machine to RemoteSigned, so unsigned local scripts can run. The Windows 11 client default is Restricted. This is a convenience for script authors, not a performance tweak.
whoBenefits: Developers and admins who run their own unsigned scripts; not a general recommendation
tradeoff: Weakens the script execution policy: any local unsigned script can run. On managed devices policy from Intune, AppLocker or WDAC normally controls this.
managedDeviceImpact: Conflicts with execution-policy settings pushed by Intune or Group Policy.

description: Hardware clock is UTC (dual boot only).
breaks: Clock offset on Windows-only systems
explanation: Hardware clock is UTC (dual boot only).
whoBenefits: Users with a specific need
tradeoff: Clock offset on Windows-only systems

description: Enable inline sudo (24H2+).
explanation: Enable inline sudo (24H2+).
whoBenefits: Users with a specific need
tradeoff: None documented.

description: Disable SysMain (Superfetch) service.
measuredEffect: not measured on SSD/NVMe; the only pro-disable report (Tech Community) counts standby cache as used RAM. Engadget and HelpDeskGeek: only worth trying on HDD or under 4 GB RAM.
explanation: SysMain pre-loads frequently used apps into memory. It was designed for slow hard drives and does little on SSD or NVMe drives. The only report of a gain counts standby memory as used, but standby memory is free memory: Windows hands it to apps on demand, so a high figure there is not a problem. Engadget and HelpDeskGeek advise leaving SysMain on except on an HDD or under 4 GB of RAM.
whoBenefits: SSD/NVMe users who want fewer background disk reads; not HDD users
tradeoff: On a hard drive, app launches and boot can get slower.

description: Set Windows Search (WSearch) to Manual instead of Automatic.
measuredEffect: one reviewer: nearly 1 GB on a 16 GB laptop (single machine, unrepeated); Microsoft: normal is a few hundred MB. Microsoft KB 4558579: typical index under 30,000 items, issues above 400,000; GB-level indexer memory points to a corrupted index (rebuild).
explanation: The Windows Search indexer can use a lot of memory when its index is large or corrupted; one reviewer reported over 1 GB freed, though Microsoft says a few hundred MB is normal. Microsoft favours rebuilding the index over disabling. Manual start is gentler than Disabled.
whoBenefits: People with a huge or broken index who use a separate search tool; first try rebuilding the index
tradeoff: Slower Start/Explorer search, Outlook search may degrade, and server-side search for SMB shares depends on it.

description: Disable the Print Spooler service on PCs that never print.
measuredEffect: not measured for RAM; security benefit documented by Microsoft
explanation: Mainly a security hardening step: the Print Spooler has been a repeated attack target, and Microsoft recommends disabling it on domain controllers and admin systems. It saves almost no memory. Do not use if you print, including to PDF printers that rely on the spooler.
whoBenefits: Non-printing PCs, domain controllers, admin workstations
tradeoff: No local or remote printing; check dependencies first.

description: Keep Remote Registry disabled.
breaks: Remote management, inventory and monitoring tools that read the registry remotely (for example some ConfigMgr and RMM tools).
explanation: Remote Registry lets other machines read your registry over the network. It is a security hardening item (it appears in CIS benchmarks), not a performance one, and it is disabled by default on most client installs. Remote management tools such as Configuration Manager need it.
whoBenefits: Home PCs and hardened machines; not managed fleets
tradeoff: Breaks remote management tools that use the remote registry.
managedDeviceImpact: Remote management or inventory tools used by your IT team may stop working.

description: Disable Downloaded Maps Manager (MapsBroker).
explanation: Handles offline map downloads for the Maps app. It is idle unless you use offline maps, so there is no real gain, but it is listed in CIS hardening.
whoBenefits: Hardening-minded users
tradeoff: Offline Maps stop updating.

description: Restore system-wide timer resolution requests (GlobalTimerResolutionRequests=1) so one app's high-resolution timer request applies to all processes, as before Windows 10 2004.
breaks: Battery life on laptops; slightly higher idle power on desktops.
measuredEffect: not measured; tools such as MeasureSleep show Sleep() precision changes, but no input-lag or frame-time benefit was documented
explanation: Since Windows 10 2004 only the program that asks for a faster timer gets it; other programs stay at about 15.6 ms. This value makes requests system-wide again. Microsoft says higher resolution can reduce overall performance, use more power and block CPU power saving. No instrumented before/after latency numbers were found.
whoBenefits: Users who run a timer-sensitive app and depend on other processes seeing the fast timer; mostly audio or legacy-software cases
tradeoff: More CPU wakeups, higher idle power and battery drain, and possibly lower throughput.

description: Turn off per-user Game DVR app capture and background (historical) recording.
measuredEffect: Laptopmedia: about 0.3 FPS difference, within noise (GTA V, MX150).
explanation: Switches off Game Bar app capture and the always-on background recording buffer for your account only. Measured cost of recording is about 0.3 FPS on a weak laptop, so expect a small gain mainly on low-end PCs.
whoBenefits: Budget or older PCs that never use Game Bar clips
tradeoff: No Win+Alt+G background clips; Game Bar recording features stop working.

description: Turn off all Windows Spotlight features (lock screen Spotlight, tips and suggestions) for the current user by policy.
explanation: Microsoft documents this policy as the switch that turns off every Windows Spotlight feature, including lock-screen ads and tips, for a user. It is about a quieter, ad-free screen and a bit less network traffic, not speed.
whoBenefits: Anyone who wants the lock screen and Settings free of promotions and rotating suggestions; metered links
tradeoff: The lock screen falls back to a picture or slideshow. Microsoft's table shows the matching policy as not supported on Pro, and it does not cover per-user Settings toggles, so the effect may be limited there.

description: Cap Delivery Optimization monthly upload to 5 GB instead of the 20 GB default, keeping peering but bounding upstream use.
measuredEffect: No measurement found (the 20 GB figure is Microsoft's default cap, not a measured effect).
explanation: Limits how much your PC may upload to other PCs per month (5 GB instead of the 20 GB default). Redundant if net-delivery-optimization-off is applied: with DODownloadMode=0 there is no peering, so there is nothing to cap.
whoBenefits: Home users on capped or slow upstream connections.
tradeoff: Peers get fewer shares from your PC once the cap is reached. Pointless if peer-to-peer is already off.

description: Limit Delivery Optimization background downloads to 25 percent of measured bandwidth (default is dynamic, up to 45 percent).
explanation: Keeps background update downloads from using most of your connection. Microsoft says throttling is the supported way to reduce DO network load, as turning DO off does not stop downloads.
whoBenefits: Users who notice lag during background updates.
tradeoff: Background updates download more slowly.

description: Stop the Maps settings page from generating untriggered network traffic.
explanation: Documented by Microsoft as the companion to the automatic map update policy. It prevents map traffic when you merely open the Settings page.
whoBenefits: Privacy-minded users.
tradeoff: None meaningful; Maps keeps working.

description: Hide the Recommended section of the Start menu (recent files and suggested items) using the documented Start policy.
explanation: Removes the Recommended area of Start, where Windows shows recent files and suggested apps and sites. Documented by Microsoft as a policy from Windows 11 22H2, so it is the official route rather than a hack. A cleaner, less ad-prone Start, not a speed gain.
whoBenefits: Anyone who wants a minimal Start menu.
tradeoff: You lose quick access to recently opened files from Start. Reports differ on edition support; Microsoft's CSP table lists Pro.

description: Disable Paint AI features (Cocreator, Generative Fill, Image Creator) by device policy.
explanation: Switches off the AI image tools inside Paint while keeping Paint itself. These policies live in a separate Paint key, not the WindowsAI key.
whoBenefits: Users who want Paint without cloud AI features.
tradeoff: You lose Cocreator, Generative Fill and Image Creator. Needs a recent Paint and Windows update.

description: Block AI features (Rewrite, summarise) in Notepad by policy.
explanation: Notepad's AI text tools are on by default on managed devices. This policy blocks them. Microsoft's page names the policy DisableAIFeaturesInNotepad but gives the registry value as DisableAIFeatures, so test on one machine first.
whoBenefits: People who want Notepad as a plain editor.
tradeoff: You lose Rewrite and related AI helpers. The value name is inconsistent in the docs; verify the AI buttons disappear. Needs Notepad 11.2503.16.0 or later.

description: Turn off lock screen widgets via the Dsh policy.
explanation: Removes widgets such as weather from the lock screen. Microsoft labels this policy as Insider Preview, so it may not take effect on every build. The wider AllowNewsAndInterests=0 policy covers the whole Widgets experience.
whoBenefits: Users who want a clean lock screen.
tradeoff: Insider-only per Microsoft Learn; no effect on release builds until it ships. No weather or widget info on the lock screen once it applies.

description: Hide the Copilot Chat icon in the Edge toolbar (Entra ID profiles).
explanation: Sets the documented Edge policy Microsoft365CopilotChatIconEnabled to 0, which hides the Copilot Chat icon (Edge 139 and later, Entra ID profiles only). Page-context handling is a separate tweak.
whoBenefits: Edge users signed in with a work or school account.
tradeoff: Only applies to Entra ID profiles. The icon is hidden; Copilot itself is not removed.

description: Stop Edge Copilot reading page context for Entra ID users (also disables Microsoft 365 link auto-open in Copilot).
breaks: Copilot page-context features for licensed Entra users.
explanation: Sets EdgeEntraCopilotPageContext to 0. Besides stopping Copilot from reading the page you are on, Microsoft documents that this also turns off M365LinksAutoOpenCopilotEnabled, so Microsoft 365 links no longer open in Copilot, for licensed Entra users.
whoBenefits: Organisations or users who do not want Copilot to read page content
tradeoff: A functional change, not just hiding an icon: Copilot page summaries and Microsoft 365 link handoff stop working for Entra ID profiles.
managedDeviceImpact: Overrides an Edge policy your admin may have set; check edge://policy.

description: Stop Outlook prompting users to migrate to the new Outlook.
explanation: Disables the automatic migration to the new Outlook for Windows in classic Outlook. It does not stop the new Outlook app being preinstalled: Microsoft says that cannot be blocked on builds after 23H2.
whoBenefits: Classic Outlook users.
tradeoff: Only helps with classic Outlook; the new app remains installed.

description: Lock Chrome Memory Saver on by policy (HighEfficiencyModeEnabled).
measuredEffect: One independent test (Benchmark.pl, n=1): Chrome 1414 MB at start, about 7.5% lower after 40 min, about 83% lower after a long idle. Google claims up to 40% (vendor). Memory Saver is on by default in recent Chrome; the policy locks it on.
explanation: Memory Saver discards background tabs after a period of inactivity, which frees their memory. Tabs that play audio or video, share the screen, have partly filled forms, run downloads or are pinned are kept.
whoBenefits: People with many Chrome tabs open, such as 100+ processes on a 16-32 GB PC
tradeoff: Discarded tabs reload when you switch back to them. Users cannot turn Memory Saver off while the policy is set; the savings level stays user-controlled.

description: Set Chrome Memory Saver to the Maximum savings level (MemorySaverModeSavings = 2).
measuredEffect: not measured for the Maximum level; see chrome-memory-saver-on for the default level
explanation: Turns Memory Saver on and sets the Maximum savings level, so background tabs go inactive sooner than at the Moderate default. Needs Chrome 126 or later. Pick this or chrome-memory-saver-on, not both.
whoBenefits: People who still run short of memory with the default Memory Saver level
tradeoff: Tabs go inactive sooner and reload more often, which costs network and time.

description: Stop Chrome from running in the background after the last window is closed (BackgroundModeEnabled = 0).
measuredEffect: not measured; prevents Chrome processes staying resident after the last window closes
explanation: By default Chrome can keep a background process alive after you close the last window so apps and extensions keep running. The policy turns that off, so closing Chrome ends its processes and frees their memory.
whoBenefits: Chrome users who close the browser and expect its memory to be released
tradeoff: Chrome apps and extensions that rely on running in the background (some notification and sync features) stop when Chrome is closed.

description: Recommend Edge sleeping tabs on with a 5-minute timeout (user-overridable defaults).
measuredEffect: Microsoft telemetry: about 39.1 MB saved per slept tab on average (6 billion tabs over 28 days); Edge 100 claim of 85% memory per slept tab. Default timeout is 900 s; this sets 300 s.
explanation: Sleeping tabs are on by default. This sets a recommended (user-overridable) default and shortens the timeout from 15 to 5 minutes. Edge heuristics skip tabs that play audio, stream or show notifications.
whoBenefits: People with many Edge tabs open in the background
tradeoff: Idle tabs wake with a short delay. Does not apply to Edge profiles signed in with a personal Microsoft account (Learn: Applies to a profile that is signed in with a Microsoft account: No). On managed devices Intune may already set these.

description: Cap Edge memory at 4 GB (TotalMemoryLimitMb = 4096, mandatory policy).
measuredEffect: not measured; Microsoft: no guarantee the browser stays under the limit; without the policy Edge only saves memory when physical memory is low
explanation: Sets a memory limit for the Edge browser. Once Edge passes the limit it discards tabs to get back under it. Only the mandatory path is supported; the Recommended path does not work for this policy.
whoBenefits: PCs where Edge grows past several GB and crowds out other programs
tradeoff: Tabs are discarded and fully reloaded once Edge passes 4 GB; heavy web apps may lose state.
